title: I'm Not Good at Much
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart argues for radical focus in professional development, both for individual teachers and for school leaders planning PD: rather than trying to be excellent at everything, aim to be average at most things and truly excellent at only a handful of high-leverage practices. He illustrates with Early Career Dave, who wanted to be the National Teacher of the Year and modeled himself on idealized teacher-heroes, and who burned out because that approach to the career left no room for a life outside the classroom. After returning to teaching, he committed to a narrower set of fundamentals questions, starting from what's school for and working down to concrete instructional priorities, rather than chasing every new idea or shiny initiative. The piece closes with a direct appeal to school leaders currently planning next year's PD: give teachers explicit permission to go deep on a small number of things rather than spreading effort thin across many.
points: Core argument: excellence in a handful of strategically chosen areas, paired with being merely average everywhere else, produces a more sustainable and ultimately more effective teaching career than trying to be excellent at everything.

The Early Career Dave narrative, modeling himself on Erin Gruwell, Ron Clark, and Dead Poets Society's teacher-hero, is used as a cautionary case: that approach was well-suited for a monk but not well-suited for a husband or father, and it led him to quit.
His recovery strategy was a chain of burning questions starting from the purpose of school and working down to concrete daily priorities, rather than chasing new ideas as they appeared.
Direct ask to school leaders: when planning next year's PD, give teachers explicit permission to focus improvement efforts on as few things as possible rather than spreading initiatives thin.
quotes: A key to my teaching career so far is that I've decided to be average at most things and excellent at only a handful. In many areas of teaching, I'm just okay. But in what I have found to be the most strategic areas, I've gained a deep understanding and proficiency.

The problem is, that guy had to quit. There was no way to teach like he taught and have a life outside the classroom. His approach to the career was well-suited for a monk but not well-suited for a husband or father.
I couldn't chase the latest shiny object. I couldn't complete all the project ideas that popped into my mind when I was inspired. Instead, I had to apprentice myself to the fundamentals of our craft.

It is super basic on purpose. Because when you focus on the basics, you develop a deep grasp of how the basics work. And once you have that grasp, you become capable of instructional and curricular decision-making that would've been impossible for you before you apprenticed to the basics.
And if you're not a PD decision-maker, I hope you'll take this away: the basics matter. They are enough. It's more than okay to be okay at most things but excellent at only the important few.
